tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

20	// leading slash. owner/repo reuse the GitHub identifier charsets from

27	// ref grammar: mirrorCloneURL still spells the token inline, because its doc

39	// git-remote-entire resolves directly. Such a URL already names the cluster, so
40	// `repo clone` passes it through to `git clone` untouched.
41	const entireCloneURLScheme = "entire://"

43	// isEntireCloneURL reports whether ref is a full entire:// clone URL (vs. the
44	// `/gh/<owner>/<repo>` shorthand that needs a mirror lookup).
45	func isEntireCloneURL(ref string) bool {
46		return strings.HasPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(ref), entireCloneURLScheme)
47	}
48	
49	// mirrorCloneURL synthesizes the entire:// clone URL for a GitHub mirror from
50	// its cluster host and owner/repo — the form `git clone` accepts, which the
51	// mirror list API doesn't return. Shared by the mirror table view (mirrorRow)
52	// and `repo clone` so the wire format lives in one place.
53	//
54	// HARDCODED ASSUMPTIONS (revisit if either stops holding):
55	//   - The provider path segment is fixed to "gh". Mirrors are GitHub-only
56	//     today; the list/index API (RepoPlacement) records no provider, so there
57	//     is nothing to key off. If a non-GitHub provider ever lands, this must
58	//     take a provider argument or the URL will lie.
59	//   - This is a client-side RECONSTRUCTION, not the server's canonical URL.
60	//     The list index gives only a cluster slug, so callers resolve slug->host
61	//     (clusterHostBySlug, via a separate ListClusters call) before calling
62	//     this. If /repos ever returns the clone URL (or host+provider) directly,
63	//     drop this synthesis and that extra round-trip.
64	func mirrorCloneURL(host, owner, repo string) string {
65		return fmt.Sprintf("%s%s/gh/%s/%s", entireCloneURLScheme, host, owner, repo)

73	// as enforced by entiredb `core/resource/project_name.go` (normalizeName, behind
74	// both the repo-create path and the admin handlers):

76	//   - project: 3–32 characters of letters, digits and '-', no leading or

111	//

116		segs := strings.Split(trimRefPrefix(ref), "/")
117		if segs[0] != nativeCloneForge {
118			return "", "", fmt.Errorf("not a native ref: expected the %s/ forge token", nativeCloneForge)

128		// fails the shape check as an empty name rather than passing as a dotted
129		// one. See gitDirSuffix for why the suffix is never part of a name.
130		repo = strings.TrimSuffix(repo, gitDirSuffix)
131		if !nativeProjectRe.MatchString(project) {
132			return "", "", fmt.Errorf("project %q is not a name the server accepts: 3-32 characters of letters, digits and '-', not starting or ending with '-'", project)
133		}
134		if !nativeRepoRe.MatchString(repo) || strings.Contains(repo, "..") {
135			return "", "", fmt.Errorf("repo %q is not a name the server accepts: 1-64 characters of letters, digits, '.' and '-', not starting or ending with '.' or '-', and with no consecutive dots", repo)
136		}
137		return project, repo, nil
138	}

145	// resolveNativeRepo performs the canonical /et/<project>/<repo> identity
146	// lookup shared by clone and repo-scoped data commands.
147	func resolveNativeRepo(ctx context.Context, c nativeRepoResolverClient, project, repoName string) (*coreapi.Repo, error) {
148		repoID, err := resolveRepoRef(ctx, c, repoName, project)
149		if err != nil {
150			return nil, err
151		}
152		repo, err := c.GetRepo(ctx, coreapi.GetRepoParams{RepoId: repoID})
153		if err != nil {
154			return nil, fmt.Errorf("get repo: %w", err)
155		}
156		return repo, nil

159	// resolveNativeCloneURL resolves an Entire-native repo (by project and repo
160	// name) to its entire:// clone URL: name → ULID via the project-scoped lookup,
161	// then GetRepo — the one call that returns both clusterHost and path. The URL
162	// is the server's own coordinates via repoRemoteURL, never synthesized from the
163	// user's ref. repoName arrives with any `.git` suffix already dropped by the
164	// parser (see gitDirSuffix).
165	func resolveNativeCloneURL(ctx context.Context, c *coreapi.Client, project, repoName string) (string, error) {
166		repo, err := resolveNativeRepo(ctx, c, project, repoName)
167		if err != nil {
168			return "", err
169		}
170		cloneURL := repoRemoteURL(*repo)
171		if cloneURL == "" {
172			return "", fmt.Errorf("repo %s/%s has no clone URL yet (still provisioning?)", project, repoName)
173		}
174		// The host is server-provided but interpolated into the entire:// clone URL,
175		// so apply the same anti-token-leak guard as the mirror path (see the
176		// validateClusterHost call on the /gh/ branch).
177		if err := validateClusterHost(repo.ClusterHost.Or("")); err != nil {
178			return "", fmt.Errorf("repo has an invalid cluster host %q: %w", repo.ClusterHost.Or(""), err)
179		}
180		return cloneURL, nil
181	}

183	// gitDirSuffix is the suffix git tools habitually append to a repo path, and
184	// Entire treats it as never part of a repo name — on either backend. Every ref
185	// parser in this package drops it before the name is used; `gitremote` trims
186	// the same suffix independently, because it cannot import this package, so a
187	// change here has to be mirrored at gitremote.splitOwnerRepo.
188	//
189	// It is unsupported rather than merely unusual. GitHub rejects a name ending in
190	// `.git` outright, so for a mirror the suffix can only ever be decoration. A
191	// native repo genuinely CAN be named "foo.git" server-side (an interior dot,
192	// which is also what makes `entire-trails.el` legal), but the CLI reads every
193	// remote back through gitremote.splitOwnerRepo, which trims the suffix
194	// unconditionally — so such a repo is unaddressable by name after cloning it
195	// anyway, in trails, `api`, experts, recap and explain alike. Rather than have
196	// `repo clone` be the one path that keeps the suffix, the whole CLI drops it,
197	// and `repo create` refuses to mint a name that ends in it.
198	//
199	// The escape hatches for a native "foo.git" that already exists are its ULID
200	// and the full `entire://` URL, which `repo clone` forwards to git verbatim.
201	const gitDirSuffix = ".git"
202	
203	// trimRefPrefix normalizes a ref for segment work: surrounding space gone, one
204	// optional leading slash gone. Every place that reads a ref's leading token
205	// goes through it, so the parsers and invalidCloneRefError's dispatch cannot
206	// disagree about what the first segment is — three near-copies of this, one of
207	// them missing the TrimSpace, is what made "the token check IS the dispatch
208	// test" true only because RunE happened to trim first.
209	func trimRefPrefix(ref string) string {
210		return strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(ref), "/")
211	}
212	
213	// declaresForge reports whether ref opens with a forge token (leading slash
214	// optional). Declaring a token is what says the user meant that grammar, so a
215	// malformed ref gets that parser's reason — the bad owner, project or repo name
216	// — instead of a list of every shape `repo clone` accepts.
217	func declaresForge(ref, token string) bool {
218		return strings.HasPrefix(trimRefPrefix(ref), token+"/")
219	}
220	
221	// bareRefSuggestions returns the forge-qualified refs a bare `<a>/<b>` could
222	// have meant — one per grammar that would actually accept it, so a suggestion
223	// is never itself a ref that would fail next. Nil unless ref is exactly two
224	// slash-separated segments.
225	//
226	// This is the input the removed `<project>/<repo>` shorthand used to take
227	// (#2252), so it is what arrives from habit, and both forges take that shape.
228	// Naming both candidates is the honest answer: the ambiguity is precisely why
229	// the shorthand went, so guessing one would reintroduce it, and printing the
230	// whole grammar makes the reader do the substitution themselves. Re-running the
231	// parsers rather than re-deriving their charsets is what keeps the two in step.
232	func bareRefSuggestions(ref string) []string {
233		trimmed := trimRefPrefix(ref)
234		if strings.Count(trimmed, "/") != 1 {
235			return nil
236		}
237		var out []string
238		native := "/" + nativeCloneForge + "/" + trimmed
239		if _, _, err := parseNativeCloneRef(native); err == nil {
240			out = append(out, native)
241		}
242		mirror := "/" + mirrorCloneForge + "/" + trimmed
243		if _, _, _, err := parseMirrorCloneRef(mirror); err == nil {
244			out = append(out, mirror)
245		}
246		return out
247	}
248	
249	// cloneRefShapes lists every ref shape `repo clone` accepts, for error text.
250	const cloneRefShapes = "/et/<project>/<repo>, /gh/<owner>/<repo>, or a full entire:// URL"
251	
252	// invalidCloneRefError explains why ref matched none of the clone grammars, in
253	// four descending degrees of confidence about what the user meant: a ref that
254	// names github.com is pointed at the `/gh/` form it should have been; a ref
255	// that declared a forge token keeps the reason its own parser gave (a bad
256	// owner, project or repo name, a dot-only repo, a missing segment); a bare pair
257	// that either grammar would accept is offered both readings; and anything left
258	// gets the list of accepted shapes.
259	//
260	// Declaring a token is the whole test for showing a parser's reason: for every
261	// other ref both parsers failed only because it was not their grammar, so
262	// neither reason describes anything the user did.
263	func invalidCloneRefError(ref string, nativeErr, mirrorErr error) error {
264		// Host-qualified forms only — an unqualified `x/y` names no forge, and the
265		// suggestion branch below handles it without guessing one. A truncated
266		// `gh/foo` would otherwise read as owner "gh", and the parser's dot-only
267		// guard keeps `github.com/foo/..` out of the hint.
268		if owner, repo, err := parseHostedGitHubURL(ref); err == nil {
269			return fmt.Errorf("invalid <repo> %q: pass GitHub mirrors as /gh/%s/%s", ref, owner, repo)
270		}
271		if declaresForge(ref, mirrorCloneForge) {
272			return fmt.Errorf("invalid <repo> %q: %w", ref, mirrorErr)
273		}
274		if declaresForge(ref, nativeCloneForge) {
275			return fmt.Errorf("invalid <repo> %q: %w", ref, nativeErr)
276		}
277		if s := bareRefSuggestions(ref); len(s) > 0 {
278			return fmt.Errorf("invalid <repo> %q: a ref must name its forge — did you mean %s?", ref, strings.Join(s, " or "))
279		}
280		return fmt.Errorf("invalid <repo> %q: expected %s", ref, cloneRefShapes)
281	}
282	
283	// parseMirrorCloneRef turns a clone ref like `/gh/entirehq/entire-api` into the
284	// API provider ("github") and the lowercased owner/repo. The `gh` token is the
285	// path provider used in entire:// clone URLs; it maps to the "github" upstream
286	// provider the control plane records.
287	func parseMirrorCloneRef(ref string) (provider, owner, repo string, err error) {
288		m := mirrorCloneRefRe.FindStringSubmatch(strings.TrimSpace(ref))
289		if m == nil {
290			return "", "", "", fmt.Errorf("expected gh/<owner>/<repo> (leading slash optional; owner: letters, digits, '-'; repo: letters, digits, '.', '_', '-'), got %q", ref)
291		}
292		owner, repo = strings.ToLower(m[1]), strings.ToLower(m[2])
293		// Drop `.git` (see gitDirSuffix) BEFORE the dot-only guard, which is what
294		// keeps `..git` — not dot-only as typed — from resolving to a "." repo.
295		repo = strings.TrimSuffix(repo, gitDirSuffix)
296		if repo == "" {
297			return "", "", "", fmt.Errorf("repo name is empty once the %s suffix is dropped: %s", gitDirSuffix, ref)
298		}
299		if gitHubDotOnlyRe.MatchString(repo) {
300			return "", "", "", fmt.Errorf("repo cannot be dot-only: %s", ref)
301		}
302		return mirrorCloneProviderGitHub, owner, repo, nil
303	}

305	func newRepoCloneCmd() *cobra.Command {
306		var cluster string
307		cmd := &cobra.Command{
308			Use:   "clone <repo> [target-dir]",
309			Short: "Clone an Entire repository",
310			Long: "Clone an Entire-native repo by its `/et/<project>/<repo>` ref, a " +
311				"GitHub mirror by its `/gh/<owner>/<repo>` ref, or a full `entire://` " +
312				"clone URL.\n\n" +
313				"A native ref resolves the repo's home cluster and clones from there " +
314				"(--cluster doesn't apply).\n\n" +
315				"With a `/gh/<owner>/<repo>` ref, looks up where the repo is mirrored: if " +
316				"it's on a single cluster, clones it directly; if it's mirrored on more " +
317				"than one, prompts you to pick which to clone from (or pass --cluster to " +
318				"choose non-interactively).\n\n" +
319				"A full `entire://` URL already names the cluster, so it's passed straight " +
320				"through to `git clone` with no lookup (and --cluster is ignored). The " +
321				"optional [target-dir] is passed through to `git clone` either way.",
322			Example: "  entire repo clone /et/project/example\n" +
323				"  entire repo clone /gh/entirehq/entire-api\n" +
324				"  entire repo clone /gh/entirehq/entire-api ./entire-api\n" +
325				"  entire repo clone /gh/entirehq/entire-api --cluster aws-us-east-2.entire.io\n" +
326				"  entire repo clone entire://aws-us-east-2.entire.io/gh/entirehq/entire-api",
327			Args: cobra.RangeArgs(1, 2),
328			RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
329				cmd.SilenceUsage = true
330				// Trim once up front so the entire:// detection and the value forwarded
331				// to git clone agree (the shorthand path trims inside parseMirrorCloneRef).
332				ref := strings.TrimSpace(args[0])
333				var targetDir string
334				if len(args) > 1 {
335					targetDir = args[1]
336				}
337	
338				// A full entire:// clone URL already embeds the cluster host (it's what
339				// --cluster would otherwise resolve to), so pass it verbatim to git clone
340				// — no mirror lookup or cluster resolution. --cluster is irrelevant here.
341				//
342				// Deliberately NOT run through validateClusterHost: this is a raw URL the
343				// user typed, forwarded to `git clone` exactly as given (the whole point
344				// of this branch), so it's equivalent to running `git clone entire://…`
345				// directly. The validateClusterHost guard applies on the shorthand path
346				// where we *synthesize* the URL from a --cluster flag or an API-supplied
347				// host — values that flow into the STS audience under our own construction.
348				if isEntireCloneURL(ref) {
349					return runGitClone(cmd.Context(), cmd, ref, targetDir)
350				}
351	
352				// Native ref: resolve the repo's home cluster via the active-context
353				// control plane and clone from there. A native repo lives on exactly
354				// one home cluster, so --cluster has nothing to choose between.
355				project, repoName, nativeErr := parseNativeCloneRef(ref)
356				if nativeErr == nil {
357					if cluster != "" {
358						return fmt.Errorf("--cluster applies to /gh/ mirror refs; %s/%s is cloned from its home cluster", project, repoName)
359					}
360					var cloneURL string
361					if err := runCore(cmd, func(ctx context.Context, c *coreapi.Client) error {
362						url, err := resolveNativeCloneURL(ctx, c, project, repoName)
363						if err != nil {
364							return err
365						}
366						cloneURL = url
367						return nil
368					}); err != nil {
369						return err
370					}
371					return runGitClone(cmd.Context(), cmd, cloneURL, targetDir)
372				}
373	
374				// provider is always "github" for the /gh/ shorthand; the pull-gated
375				// resolver pins the provider itself, so it's not threaded through.
376				_, owner, repo, mirrorErr := parseMirrorCloneRef(ref)
377				if mirrorErr != nil {
378					return invalidCloneRefError(ref, nativeErr, mirrorErr)
379				}
380	
381				var placements []coreapi.ResolvedPlacement
382				lister := func(ctx context.Context, c *coreapi.Client) error {
383					ps, err := resolvePullablePlacements(ctx, c, owner, repo)
384					if err != nil {
385						return err
386					}
387					placements = ps
388					return nil
389				}
390				// An explicit --cluster may name a cluster in a different federation
391				// than the active context, whose mirrors the active-context core can't
392				// see (the original bug: cloning a royalcanin.partial.to mirror while a
393				// different context is active failed with "not mirrored on ..."). Dial
394				// the core fronting that cluster — discovered from its well-known and
395				// authenticated with the matching local context, the same path
396				// `mirror create <url> [cluster]` uses — so the lookup resolves against
397				// the right federation. With no --cluster, list from the active context.
398				runWithCore := runCore
399				if cluster != "" {
400					if err := validateClusterHost(cluster); err != nil {
401						return fmt.Errorf("invalid --cluster: %w", err)
402					}
403					runWithCore = func(cmd *cobra.Command, fn func(context.Context, *coreapi.Client) error) error {
404						return runCoreForCluster(cmd, cluster, fn)
405					}
406				}
407				if err := runWithCore(cmd, lister); err != nil {
408					return err
409				}
410	
411				if len(placements) == 0 {
412					return fmt.Errorf("no mirror found for /gh/%s/%s; run 'entire repo mirror create github.com/%s/%s' to onboard it", owner, repo, owner, repo)
413				}
414	
415				chosen, err := selectCloneTarget(cmd, placements, cluster)
416				if err != nil {
417					return err
418				}
419	
420				// chosen.ClusterHost is server-provided, but it's interpolated into the
421				// entire:// clone URL just like the user-supplied --cluster, so apply the
422				// same anti-token-leak guard (validateClusterHost) before building it —
423				// defense-in-depth against a malformed host reaching git / the STS audience.
424				if err := validateClusterHost(chosen.ClusterHost); err != nil {
425					return fmt.Errorf("mirror has an invalid cluster host %q: %w", chosen.ClusterHost, err)
426				}
427				cloneURL := mirrorCloneURL(chosen.ClusterHost, owner, repo)
428				return runGitClone(cmd.Context(), cmd, cloneURL, targetDir)
429			},
430		}
431		cmd.Flags().StringVar(&cluster, "cluster", "", "Cluster host to clone from when the repo is mirrored on more than one (may belong to another auth context)")
432		return cmd
433	}

435	// mirrorLister is the subset of the control-plane client listMirrorsForRepo
436	// needs. Narrowing to an interface lets callers (e.g. resolveCurrentRepoID in
437	// api_cmd.go, and entireapi_client.go's currentRepoRef) inject a fake control
438	// plane in tests; *coreapi.Client satisfies it.
439	type mirrorLister interface {
440		ListMirrors(ctx context.Context, params coreapi.ListMirrorsParams) (*coreapi.ListMirrorsOutputBody, error)
441	}
442	
443	// listMirrorsForRepo returns every mirror placement of one upstream repo across
444	// clusters. The list API filters by provider+owner server-side but has no repo
445	// filter, so the repo match is applied client-side (owner is already lowercased
446	// to match what the server persists).
447	func listMirrorsForRepo(ctx context.Context, c mirrorLister, provider, owner, repo string) ([]coreapi.Mirror, error) {
448		all, err := fetchAllPages(ctx, func(ctx context.Context, cursor string) ([]coreapi.Mirror, string, error) {
449			params := coreapi.ListMirrorsParams{
450				Provider: coreapi.NewOptString(provider),
451				Owner:    coreapi.NewOptString(owner),
452			}
453			if cursor != "" {
454				params.PageToken = coreapi.NewOptString(cursor)
455			}
456			out, err := c.ListMirrors(ctx, params)
457			if err != nil {
458				return nil, "", fmt.Errorf("list mirrors: %w", err)
459			}
460			return out.Mirrors, out.NextPageToken.Or(""), nil
461		})
462		if err != nil {
463			return nil, err
464		}
465		matched := make([]coreapi.Mirror, 0, len(all))
466		for _, m := range all {
467			if strings.EqualFold(m.Repo, repo) {
468				matched = append(matched, m)
469			}
470		}
471		return matched, nil
472	}

474	// resolvePullablePlacements returns every cluster placement of one GitHub
475	// upstream the caller may pull (clone). It backs `repo clone /gh/<owner>/<repo>`
476	// and deliberately differs from listMirrorsForRepo: that reads the
477	// affiliation-scoped mirror list (repo#list), which omits public mirrors the
478	// caller holds no grant on, so the shorthand used to fail on a public repo that
479	// clones fine by full entire:// URL. This hits the pull-gated /mirrors/placements
480	// endpoint instead — the same authority the clone's STS exchange enforces — so
481	// anything clonable resolves, public or private-with-grant.
482	//
483	// owner/repo arrive already lowercased from parseMirrorCloneRef; the server
484	// matches case-insensitively regardless. An empty result means not mirrored or
485	// not pullable, and the caller surfaces that.
486	func resolvePullablePlacements(ctx context.Context, c *coreapi.Client, owner, repo string) ([]coreapi.ResolvedPlacement, error) {
487		out, err := c.ResolveMirrorPlacements(ctx, coreapi.ResolveMirrorPlacementsParams{
488			Provider: coreapi.ResolveMirrorPlacementsProviderGithub,
489			Owner:    owner,
490			Repo:     repo,
491		})
492		if err != nil {
493			return nil, fmt.Errorf("resolve mirror placements: %w", err)
494		}
495		return out.Placements, nil
496	}

498	// placementPicker adapts selectPlacement's messages to the calling verb. The
499	// picker logic is identical for every consumer (dedupe by host, honor an
500	// explicit selector, prompt only when there's a real choice); only the words
501	// differ, so they're passed in rather than duplicated per command.
502	type placementPicker struct {
503		// selector names the non-interactive way to choose a cluster, as the user
504		// would type it (e.g. `--cluster`). Interpolated into the no-terminal error
505		// so the pointer names a flag the calling command actually accepts.
506		selector string
507		// title is the interactive single-select's prompt.
508		title string
509		// action names the operation in the cancellation message, capitalized
510		// ("Clone", "Remote update") — handleFormCancellation prints
511		// "<action> cancelled."
512		action string
513	}

515	// selectCloneTarget resolves which mirror placement to clone from, with the
516	// clone verb's wording. See selectPlacement for the selection rules.
517	func selectCloneTarget(cmd *cobra.Command, placements []coreapi.ResolvedPlacement, clusterFlag string) (coreapi.ResolvedPlacement, error) {
518		return selectPlacement(cmd, placements, clusterFlag, placementPicker{
519			selector: "--cluster",
520			title:    "This repo is mirrored on more than one cluster — pick one to clone from",
521			action:   "Clone",
522		})
523	}

525	// selectPlacement resolves which mirror placement a verb should act on. With one
526	// placement it returns it directly. With an explicit clusterSel it picks the
527	// matching one (or errors listing the available hosts). With more than one and no
528	// selector it prompts interactively, failing fast with a p.selector pointer when
529	// there's no terminal.
530	func selectPlacement(cmd *cobra.Command, placements []coreapi.ResolvedPlacement, clusterSel string, p placementPicker) (coreapi.ResolvedPlacement, error) {
531		// Dedupe by cluster host: one placement per cluster is what a caller acts on,
532		// and the same host appearing twice would only confuse the picker. Key on the
533		// case-folded host — DNS is case-insensitive, so a selector value differing
534		// only in case from the API's ClusterHost must still match (the alternative is
535		// a misleading "not mirrored on ..." after a successful lookup + dial).
536		byHost := make(map[string]coreapi.ResolvedPlacement, len(placements))
537		hosts := make([]string, 0, len(placements))
538		for _, p := range placements {
539			key := strings.ToLower(p.ClusterHost)
540			if _, seen := byHost[key]; seen {
541				continue
542			}
543			byHost[key] = p
544			hosts = append(hosts, key)
545		}
546		sort.Strings(hosts)
547	
548		if clusterSel != "" {
549			match, ok := byHost[strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(clusterSel))]
550			if !ok {
551				return coreapi.ResolvedPlacement{}, fmt.Errorf("repo is not mirrored on %q; available: %s", clusterSel, strings.Join(hosts, ", "))
552			}
553			return match, nil
554		}
555	
556		if len(hosts) == 1 {
557			return byHost[hosts[0]], nil
558		}
559	
560		if !interactive.CanPromptInteractively() {
561			return coreapi.ResolvedPlacement{}, fmt.Errorf("repo is mirrored on %d clusters; pass %s to choose one of: %s", len(hosts), p.selector, strings.Join(hosts, ", "))
562		}
563	
564		options := make([]huh.Option[string], len(hosts))
565		for i, h := range hosts {
566			options[i] = huh.NewOption(mirrorCellLabel(byHost[h]), h)
567		}
568		var selected string
569		form := NewAccessibleForm(
570			huh.NewGroup(
571				huh.NewSelect[string]().
572					Title(p.title).
573					Options(options...).
574					Value(&selected),
575			),
576		)
577		if err := form.RunWithContext(cmd.Context()); err != nil {
578			// handleFormCancellation prints "<action> cancelled." and returns nil for a
579			// Ctrl+C / cancelled-context abort. Surface that as a SilentError so the
580			// caller stops instead of falling through to act on a zero-value target
581			// (the `entire:///gh/...` empty-host bug) without main.go reprinting the
582			// message handleFormCancellation already wrote; a real form error propagates.
583			if cerr := handleFormCancellation(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), p.action, err); cerr != nil {
584				return coreapi.ResolvedPlacement{}, cerr
585			}
586			return coreapi.ResolvedPlacement{}, NewSilentError(fmt.Errorf("%s cancelled", strings.ToLower(p.action)))
587		}
588		match, ok := byHost[selected]
589		if !ok {
590			// The form succeeded but handed back a host that is not on offer. Nothing
591			// has been printed here, so this must NOT be a SilentError — main.go
592			// suppresses those, and the command would exit non-zero with no message.
593			return coreapi.ResolvedPlacement{}, fmt.Errorf("no cluster selected from the %d offered", len(hosts))
594		}
595		return match, nil
596	}

598	// mirrorCellLabel is the human label for a mirror placement in the clone picker:
599	// the physical cell and jurisdiction when known, always anchored by the cluster
600	// host that goes into the clone URL.
601	func mirrorCellLabel(p coreapi.ResolvedPlacement) string {
602		cell := strings.TrimSpace(p.Cell.Or(""))
603		jur := strings.TrimSpace(p.Jurisdiction.Or(""))
604		switch {
605		case cell != "" && jur != "":
606			return fmt.Sprintf("%s (%s) — %s", cell, jur, p.ClusterHost)
607		case cell != "":
608			return fmt.Sprintf("%s — %s", cell, p.ClusterHost)
609		default:
610			return p.ClusterHost
611		}
612	}

content.text:
The fix is small and there's really one right option. Assessment:

## Root cause

All `repo` subcommands already share one resolver — `resolveRepoRef` (`resolveref.go:217`) — used by `repo get`/`delete`, `visibility get`/`set`, `protection list`/`add`/`remove`, and `grant repo add`/`list`/`remove`. It only understands two forms: a ULID or a bare name + `--project`. The `/et/<project>/<repo>` grammar lives separately in `parseNativeCloneRef` (`repo_clone.go:115`, same package), and only `repo clone` calls it. So the "ideally share one resolver" the issue asks for already exists; it just never learned the path form.

## Options

**A. Teach `resolveRepoRef` to parse `/et/<project>/<repo>` — recommended.**
At the top of `resolveRepoRef`, try `parseNativeCloneRef(ref)`; on success, use the embedded project as the scope and recurse into the existing name lookup. ~15 lines plus tests. This fixes all ten call sites at once — get, delete, visibility, protection, and grants — which is exactly the shared-resolver shape the issue wants. Details that fall out cleanly:

- **`--project` conflict**: reject `--project` alongside an `/et/` ref ("the ref already names its project"), mirroring how clone rejects `--cluster` on native refs. Simpler than comparing the two with case folding.
- **Invariants preserved for free**: routing through `parseNativeCloneRef` keeps the namesquatting guard — a bare `<project>/<repo>` still doesn't resolve (the parser requires the `et/` token, pinned by `TestCloneRefAlwaysRequiresItsForgePrefix`), and `.git`-suffix trimming and server-shape validation come along.
- **Better errors too**: a ref that declares `et/` but is malformed gets the parser's specific reason instead of the misleading "is a name" message.

**B. Patch only `repo get`.** Smaller on paper, but the same rejection exists in delete, visibility, protection, and grants — the copy-paste loop the issue describes breaks there too. A guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than one per caller. Not worth it.

**C. Error-message-only.** Point the error at the accepted forms. Doesn't meet the issue's "Expected" section; only worth doing as part of A (where it happens naturally).

## Out of scope, worth noting in the PR

- `/gh/<owner>/<repo>` for `repo get` etc. — mirrors are resolvable via the consolidated `ListRepos` index (the `resolveRepoCellPlacement` path), but that's a separate grammar and a separate decision; the issue only asks for `/et/`.
- The server-side half (missing provider slug in routes) is ENT-2101, already tracked separately.

Want me to implement option A?

content.text:
Both good pushbacks. Here's my thinking on each.

## 1. Why reject `--project` alongside an `/et/` ref

The ref already names its project, so the flag is either redundant or contradictory — and the contradictory case flows into `repo delete`. There are three ways to handle it:

- **Reject always** (what I proposed). One `if` and a crisp message ("the /et/ ref already names its project; drop --project"). Same shape as clone rejecting `--cluster` on native refs.
- **Reject only on mismatch.** Friendlier when they agree, but "agree" isn't a string compare: `--project` accepts a ULID too, so checking agreement means resolving the flag's project (an extra control-plane round trip) or case-folding names only and having a hole for the ULID form. That's real logic to buy a case that shouldn't occur.
- **Silently prefer the ref.** Cheapest, but a user who typed `--project foo` and pasted `/et/bar/r1` gets an action on a repo in `bar` with no signal. With delete in the caller set, silent tie-breaking is the wrong default.

Since this is a brand-new input form, there's no script anywhere that passes both — rejecting always breaks nobody and never guesses. That's why. If you'd rather allow the agreeing-name case, it's doable, but I don't think it earns the comparison logic.

## 2. Never assuming a provider

Agreed, and this is the part worth being explicit about in the implementation. The repo's existing rule (#2252) is: **every ref names its forge; a bare pair resolves nowhere**. Routing through `parseNativeCloneRef` gets most of this for free — it refuses anything that doesn't literally open with the `et/` token — but there are two spots where the naive version of option A would quietly assume:

- **Bare `<a>/<b>` must keep failing.** It does: `parseNativeCloneRef` returns "not a native ref" for it, so it falls through to the name path — where it 404s after a round trip today. Slightly better: since repo names can never contain `/` (per `nativeRepoRe` / server rules), any slash-bearing ref that isn't a valid `/et/` ref can be refused locally with a "did you mean `/et/<a>/<b>`?" suggestion (the `bareRefSuggestions` pattern), never sent to the by-name lookup. No guessing — it names the candidate, the user decides.
- **`/gh/<owner>/<repo>` must not be misread.** Today it would fall into "is a name; pass --project", which is wrong twice (it's not a name, and no `--project` fixes it). The resolver should detect the `gh/` token via `declaresForge` and refuse it explicitly — "this command addresses native repos; mirrors are managed via `entire repo mirror …`" — the same shape as trails refusing `et` with `errTrailsNativeUnsupported`. We never treat `gh/x/y` as a name, and we never silently resolve it either.

So the dispatch is token-driven, exhaustive, and defaults to refusal: `et/` → parse strictly; `gh/` → targeted refusal; any other slash-bearing ref → refusal with the `/et/` suggestion if it would parse; slash-less → existing name/ULID path unchanged. No branch infers a forge.

One test to pin it: the resolver-level counterpart of `TestCloneRefAlwaysRequiresItsForgePrefix` — bare pairs and `gh/` refs never reach the name lookup or resolve.

Sound right? If so I'll implement it in that shape.

**"The ref names its project"** just means the path form carries the project inside it: in `/et/<project>/<repo>`, the middle segment *is* the project name. `/et/nativebug-0911/r1-default` says project = `nativebug-0911`, repo = `r1-default`. So `--project` alongside it is a second copy of the same fact — that's all I meant.

**On reject-always vs reject-on-mismatch:** to be precise, reject-always doesn't silently prefer anything — it errors even when the two agree, so nothing proceeds. The silent-preference hazard only exists in the third option (ignore the flag), which we both ruled out. The real difference between your version and mine is just the *agreeing* case: mine errors on redundant-but-consistent input, yours allows it.

That said, you've changed my mind, because my cost argument against mismatch-checking was wrong. I claimed comparing needs an extra round trip; it doesn't:

- The ref's embedded project name gets resolved to a ULID anyway (that's how the repo lookup works).
- If `--project` is a ULID → compare it to that resolved ULID. Free.
- If `--project` is a name → project names are globally unique and matched case-insensitively server-side, so `strings.EqualFold` against the embedded name is a sound equality test. Also free.

So reject-on-mismatch costs nothing extra, never guesses, and is friendlier: `entire repo get "$path" --project "$proj"` works when they agree, and a disagreement gets an explicit "ref says project X but --project says Y" error instead of either side winning silently.

Final shape:

- `et/` ref → parse strictly; if `--project` also given, allow on agreement, error naming both values on mismatch.
- `gh/` ref → targeted refusal pointing at `repo mirror`.
- Other slash-bearing refs → local refusal with a `/et/<a>/<b>` suggestion when that would parse; never sent to the by-name lookup.
- Slash-less name / ULID → unchanged.

Implementing that now unless you want to adjust anything.

content.text:
You're right that it's different — they just happen to occupy the same slot in the path.

**Syntactically the same role:** in `/et/<project>/<repo>` and `/gh/<owner>/<repo>`, the middle segment is the namespace that repo names are unique within. That's the only sense in which I equated them, and it's why `ForgePathLabels` exists — the code deliberately labels the segment `<project>/<repo>` for `et` and `<owner>/<repo>` for `gh` because they're not the same concept.

**Semantically different:** a GitHub owner *is* an identity — a user or org account that owns the repo. An Entire project is not an identity; it's a grouping resource that is itself owned by something else. `project create` takes `--owner <org|account> --owner-type org|account` (project.go:43-87), so the hierarchy is:

```
org or account  →  owns  →  project  →  contains  →  repo
```

Ownership and access live a level above the path segment. Two projects owned by the same org are separate repo namespaces; on GitHub the owner and the namespace are one thing.

**For our change this doesn't move anything:** the resolver only needs "which namespace do I look this repo name up in", and that's exactly what both the ref's middle segment and `--project` name. The mismatch check stays sound because project names are globally unique (case-insensitive), regardless of who owns them.

Still good to implement the shape we agreed on?

input.command:
git checkout -b nina/cor-1632-cli-repo-get-rejects-the-etprojectrepo-path-that-repo-clone && git add cmd/entire/cli/repo.go cmd/entire/cli/resolveref.go cmd/entire/cli/resolveref_test.go && git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
Accept /et/<project>/<repo> paths in every repo-ref command

The API returns a repo's identity as a path ("/et/<project>/<repo>") and
`repo clone` accepts it, but every other repo-ref command (get, delete,
visibility, protection, grant repo) rejected it as "a name", breaking the
read-a-repo-copy-its-path loop (COR-1632).

All those commands already share resolveRepoRef, so teach it the path
grammar there: a slash-bearing ref is dispatched to the native parser
(reusing parseNativeCloneRef, so leading-slash tolerance, .git trimming,
and server-shape validation come along) and never sent to the by-name
lookup, which cannot match a slash anyway.

The #2252 rule — every ref names its forge — holds at the resolver: a
bare <a>/<b> is refused with a /et/ suggestion rather than read as
native, and a /gh/ mirror ref gets a targeted refusal pointing at
`entire repo mirror` instead of the misleading "is a name" error.

--project alongside a path ref is checked for agreement rather than
trusted or ignored: a name compares case-insensitively (the server
matches lower(name); project names are globally unique), a ULID against
the resolved project id — neither costs an extra round trip. A mismatch
is an error naming both values, since the callers include delete.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)"
